entries.meaning: Mastering her grief, Kauśalyā said: “Son, the guru’s command is wholesome medicine; honor it and act upon it as beneficial. Recognize the course of time and abandon sorrow. Raghupati is lord of the forest, Indra of heaven, and you must be lord of men—why, child, should you be so afraid? Relatives, subjects, ministers, and all the mothers: you alone, son, are the support of everyone. Seeing Fate turned against us and the time so harsh, gather courage, dear child, for your mother’s sake. Place the guru’s command upon your head and follow it; protect the subjects and remove the family’s distress.” Bharata heard the guru’s counsel and ministers’ approval as though they were sandalwood balm upon his heart. Then he heard again his mother’s gentle speech, steeped in the simple savor of character and affection.

Bharata replied: “The guru has given me excellent instruction, approved by subjects and ministers alike. Mother too has given a proper command, and I certainly wish to carry it upon my head. Hearing beneficial words from guru, father, mother, or master, one should act upon them gladly, knowing them to be good. If one first debates whether they are fitting, righteousness departs and the burden of sin falls on one’s head. But you surely give only that candid teaching which, when practiced, will be for my good. Though I understand this clearly, my heart still finds no satisfaction. Now hear my petition and give instruction suited to me. Allow me to answer and forgive the offense, for holy people do not count the faults and virtues of one in pain. With father in heaven and Sītā and Rāma in the forest, you tell me to rule: from this should I understand that you seek my welfare—or have some great task of your own?”

“My true welfare is service to Sītā’s Lord, and mother’s crookedness has taken that away. I have examined my heart and see no other means to my good. Of what account are this assembly of grief and the kingdom without seeing the feet of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā? Clothes without the body are useless, and ornaments merely burdens; metaphysical reflection without renunciation is vain. Abundant pleasures are wasted on a diseased body, as recitation and yoga are without devotion to Hari. A lovely body is futile without life, and everything of mine is futile without Raghurāya. Give me permission to go to Rāma; this alone is to my benefit. If you insist on making me king for my good, that too is said under the deluding dullness of affection. You desire happiness for a shameless, perverse-minded son of Kaikeyī, one turned from Rāma, by giving a kingdom to one as low as me.”

“I speak truth; listen and believe me: only a righteous man should be king. If you force the kingdom upon me, the earth will sink to the lowest underworld. Who is a dwelling of sin equal to me, on whose account Sītā and Rāma went to the forest? The king assigned the woods to Rāma and, separated from him, departed to heaven. Fool that I am, cause of every calamity, I sit alert and listen to all this talk. Though I see the dwelling empty without Raghubīra, my life remains and bears the world’s mockery. Rāma is pure and indifferent to sensual savor, while I am greedy and hungry for dominion and enjoyment! How long can I describe this heart’s hardness, which has humbled the thunderbolt and won distinction over it? Effects grow harsher than their causes; it is no fault of mine that iron is crueler than stone, stone than bone, and the thunderbolt itself arose from bone.”

“Attached to this body born of Kaikeyī, my base, unfortunate life has gorged itself on sin. If life remains dear amid separation from the beloved, I shall yet see and hear much more. Kaikeyī gave the forest to Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā; for her husband’s supposed welfare she sent him to heaven. She took widowhood and infamy for herself, gave the subjects grief and torment, and gave me pleasure, fair fame, and good government—Kaikeyī has accomplished everyone’s business! What further good could there be for me that you now propose to give me the royal mark? Having been born from Kaikeyī’s womb, nothing is inappropriate for me. Fate itself has shaped the whole affair for me; why make the subjects and council my accomplices? Tell me what remedy exists for someone first seized by a planet, then afflicted by wind, then stung by a scorpion, and finally made to drink wine.”

“Whatever worldly station befits Kaikeyī’s son, clever Brahmā has given precisely that to me. Fate gave me the empty distinction of being Daśaratha’s son and Rāma’s younger brother. You all tell me to bring out the coronation mark, saying the king’s command is good for everyone. In what way and to whom can I answer? Speak freely, each according to preference. Apart from my wicked mother and me, tell me whom anyone will call a benefactor in this affair. Who besides me among all moving and unmoving beings does not hold Sītā and Rāma dearer than life? Everyone’s greatest loss is my great gain; this is my misfortune, no one else’s fault. You are governed by doubt, propriety, and affection, so everything you say is appropriate. Rāma’s mother, exceptionally candid-hearted, speaks naturally under affection after seeing my wretchedness.”

“The world knows the guru as an ocean of discernment, to whom the universe is like a jujube fruit held in the hand. Yet even he prepares the coronation array for me: when Fate turns away, everyone turns away. Who in the world, apart from Rāma and Sītā, would not say that my plan lies behind this? I will supposedly hear and endure that happily—as mud inevitably gathers where water lies. I do not fear that the world will call me vile, nor do I worry about the next world. One unbearable conflagration alone dwells in my heart: because of me Sītā and Rāma suffered. Lakṣmaṇa has rightly gained life’s reward, abandoning everything and setting his mind upon Rāma’s feet. My birth has brought about Raghubara’s exile; why, unfortunate as I am, should I falsely lament? Bowing my head to everyone, I tell my terrible lowliness: without seeing Raghunātha’s feet, the burning in my heart will not go.”

entries.meaning: “No other remedy occurs to me—who understands a heart without Raghubara? One resolve alone occupies my mind: at daybreak I shall go to the Lord. Though I am harmful and guilty and every affliction arose because of me, when he sees me facing him in surrender he will forgive all and show special grace. Raghurāya is a dwelling of graciousness, reserve, perfect guilelessness, compassion, and affection. Rāma never harmed even an enemy who had harmed him; although I am a wayward child and servant, he will not reject me. If you five authorities accept my good, give me permission and blessing in gracious words, so that upon hearing my petition and recognizing me as his own servant, Rāma may return to the capital. Though born from a bad mother and always foolish and faulty, I trust Raghubīra will know me as his own and not abandon me.”

Bharata’s words pleased everyone, as though immersed in the nectar of love for Rāma. The people, scorched by the fierce poison of separation, awoke as if upon hearing an empowered mantra. Mothers, ministers, guru, and the city’s women and men were all profoundly overwhelmed by affection. Praising Bharata repeatedly, they said he embodied love for Rāma. “Dear Bharata, why would you not speak so? Rāma is dear to you as life. Any wretch who, through personal dullness, attributes your mother’s crookedness to you will live in hell for a hundred aeons with millions of people like himself. A jewel does not absorb the serpent’s sin or faults; it removes poison and burns away suffering and poverty.” They agreed that everyone should certainly go to the forest where Rāma was: Bharata had made a good proposal and given support to all who were drowning in the ocean of grief.

No small joy arose in every heart, like cātaka birds and peacocks hearing thunderclouds. Seeing that departure at dawn had been firmly settled, Bharata became dear as life to everyone. The citizens bowed to the sage and to Bharata and, after taking leave, all went home, praising Bharata’s blessed life, character, and affection as they walked. They told each other that a great task had been accomplished and began preparing everything needed for the whole populace to go. Whoever was ordered to remain as guard at home felt as if a sword had been drawn across the neck. Some said no one should be told to stay—who in the world did not desire the gain of true life? Let property, home comforts, friends, mother, father, and brother burn if they do not become a hundredfold help when one comes face-to-face with Rāma’s feet.
